description: Ground truth for evaluating ARVE. Every finding here was planted deliberately.
verification_method: osv.dev /v1/query, with every returned advisory re-checked against its own affected ranges

findings.tests: baseline detection at HEAD - if this is missed, the pipeline is broken
findings.notes: Shape sk_live_ + 24 alphanumerics. Matched by a named-vendor rule, the easiest class of secret there is.

testbed.what_was_planted: Stripe live secret key hardcoded as the fallback for the STRIPE_API_KEY environment variable.

findings.tests: non-Python path; workflow YAML is sometimes skipped by path filters
findings.notes: Produces TWO gitleaks findings: aws-access-token at line 45 (the AKIA id) and generic-api-key at line 46 (the 40-char secret). The key ID uses the real AWS base32 alphabet (A-Z, 2-7); gitleaks rejects AKIA values containing 0/1/8/9, so a naively random value is silently undetectable.

testbed.what_was_planted: AWS access key ID and secret access key set as env vars on the release-upload step.

findings.tests: a distinct Gitleaks rule class from token regexes - block detection, not a token regex
findings.notes: PEM structure is valid and passes `openssl rsa -check`, so the finding is not an artifact of a malformed file. The file carries a 3-line TESTBED header before the PEM block; openssl ignores text before the BEGIN marker (verified with `openssl rsa -check`), which is why the finding is at line 5 rather than line 1.

testbed.what_was_planted: A genuine 2048-bit RSA private key, generated throwaway with openssl and never used for anything.

findings.tests: GIT HISTORY SCANNING - absent from the working tree at HEAD, still present in history
findings.notes: VERIFIED at build time: a working-tree scan (`gitleaks dir`) reports 0 findings for this file; a history scan (`gitleaks git`) reports 1, at backend/app/settlement.py:16 in commit 5f9ec864. The file does not exist at HEAD. A scanner that only walks the filesystem misses this entirely and is wrong. ARVE must not mark it RESOLVED merely because HEAD is clean - the credential was committed and must be treated as exposed until rotated. Its value is derived deterministically by seed_history.py rather than written there as a literal, precisely so the build script does not itself put the secret at HEAD and destroy this test.

testbed.what_was_planted: SFTP password for the bank settlement-file service account.

history.deleted_message: clean up settlement config, the transfer moved to the platform job

findings.tests: FINGERPRINT BEHAVIOUR - one finding or two? Whatever ARVE does must be deliberate
findings.notes: Same 48-char value at backend/app/config.py:45 and backend/tests/conftest.py:14. Gitleaks reports TWO findings because it fingerprints per (file, line, secret). If ARVE dedupes on secret_hash alone it will report ONE; if it includes file path it will report TWO. Both are defensible - but the choice must be intentional and consistent, because it determines whether fixing one file resolves the finding or leaves it OPEN.

testbed.what_was_planted: JWT signing key, byte-for-byte identical in two different files.

findings.tests: LINE-INDEPENDENT secret_hash IDENTITY - must report the same finding, not resolve-and-reopen
findings.notes: VERIFIED at build time: a history scan reports this secret TWICE - at webhooks.py:43 in commit 4da4e7e2 and at webhooks.py:22 in commit dc9a9d69 - with a byte-identical secret value both times. Expected: ONE finding with a STABLE fingerprint that stays OPEN across the move. A fingerprint incorporating the line number will emit RESOLVED then REOPENED, a false lifecycle transition. That noise is what trains people to ignore the tool.

testbed.what_was_planted: Provider webhook signing secret that MOVES to a different line between two commits.

findings.tests: entropy rule rather than a named-vendor regex
findings.notes: No vendor prefix, so no named rule can match it; detection depends entirely on the generic-api-key keyword+entropy path. IMPORTANT: this was initially planted across three lines and was NOT detected - gitleaks requires the keyword and the value on the SAME line. It is now a single line.

testbed.what_was_planted: High-entropy 64-character key with no vendor prefix, as LEDGER_HMAC_KEY.

findings.tests: ambiguous by design - exercises the FALSE_POSITIVE / SUPPRESSED lifecycle
findings.notes: VERIFIED: gitleaks DOES report this despite the .example filename - it is not path-suppressed by default. So the ambiguity is not resolved by the scanner, it is pushed to triage. A human must decide whether a correctly-shaped credential in a template file is a real leak. This is the one finding where marking it FALSE_POSITIVE or SUPPRESSED is a legitimate outcome, and ARVE must be able to carry that state across rescans without the finding reverting to OPEN.

testbed.what_was_planted: A real-shaped SendGrid API token sitting in a committed .env.example template.

findings.tests: Markdown, non-code path - documentation is often excluded from scanning
findings.notes: Inside a fenced bash code block in a .md file. Tests that documentation paths are scanned rather than filtered out by extension.

testbed.what_was_planted: Slack incoming-webhook URL in an operational runbook.

findings.tests: baseline direct-dependency detection in the primary ecosystem
findings.notes: Lockfile is at a nested path, not the repo root. 3 GHSA records plus 3 PYSEC alias duplicates that carry no CVSS and no GitHub severity. VERIFIED in the committed baseline: osv-scanner reports this package's version as '5.1.0' although requirements.txt pins '5.1'. See normalization_notes.

findings.tests: transitive resolution depth - package is never named in requirements.in
findings.notes: Pulled in by httpx and httpcore, neither of which constrains the version. Both parents are advisory-free. osv.dev's query API also returns PYSEC-2024-230, but its ECOSYSTEM range starts at 2021.5.30 so 2018.4.16 is out of range; excluded here. VERIFIED in the committed baseline: osv-scanner DOES report PYSEC-2024-230 for this package despite the version being below that advisory's introduced bound. It is listed in the inventory as a scanner over-match so the diff comes out clean.

findings.tests: baseline detection in the second ecosystem from a nested lockfile
findings.notes: Declared at web/package.json line 12 and genuinely used by web/src/main.js.

findings.tests: lockfile graph parsing - present only in package-lock.json, absent from package.json
findings.notes: Enters solely as a dependency of http-proxy@1.18.1 (which declares ^1.0.0 and is itself advisory-free). Lock is genuine npm output; npm reports 'up to date' against it. CVE-2022-0155 was the original target but is fixed in 1.14.7 and does not apply.

findings.tests: fingerprint uniqueness per (package, advisory) - must produce TWO findings, not one
findings.notes: Exactly two advisories, no more, so the expected count is unambiguous. A fingerprint keyed only on (package, version) collapses these and loses the CRITICAL one.

findings.tests: normalize_severity - GitHub severity string 'moderate' must map to canonical MEDIUM
findings.notes: All three of this package's advisories are 'moderate', so there is no mixed-severity ambiguity. A normalizer that passes the string through or uppercases it to MODERATE is wrong on all three at once.

findings.tests: advisory with a GHSA ID but no CVE - ghsa must populate and cve must stay null
findings.notes: The package's other advisory (GHSA-hxcc-f52p-wc94) DOES carry CVE-2020-7660, so one package at one version yields one finding with a CVE and one without. Catches cve set to 'None', '', or the GHSA id. Originally assigned to http-proxy@1.18.1, but that advisory is fixed in 1.18.1 and does not apply.

findings.tests: severity fallback - OSV record has an empty severity array (no CVSS vector at all)
findings.notes: Must not crash and must not emit null. Correct result is MEDIUM via database_specific.severity='moderate'. Only single-record, no-alias, no-CVSS advisory available; PYSEC records with no severity at all always sit beside a CVSS-bearing GHSA alias, which would make the expected answer ambiguous.

expected_osv_inventory.summary: Deserialization of Untrusted Data in PyYAML

expected_osv_inventory.testbed_note: SCANNER OVER-MATCH, NOT A PLANTED FINDING. This advisory's ECOSYSTEM range is introduced 2021.5.30 / fixed 2024.7.4, so certifi 2018.4.16 is BELOW the introduced bound and is not actually affected. osv-scanner reports it anyway, most likely because the record also carries a GIT range with introduced:0. Confirmed present in the committed osv-baseline.json. ARVE reporting it is CORRECT behaviour - it faithfully reflects its scanner. Do not 'fix' ARVE to suppress this.

git_history.note: Scan the Git repository, not the filesystem. `gitleaks dir` on a working copy also walks .venv/ and node_modules/ and produces unrelated hits; both are gitignored so a repository scan does not see them.

over_matches: PYSEC-2024-230 (certifi, version below the advisory's introduced bound)
osv_baseline.note: Both lockfiles were found at nested paths; neither is at the repository root. .venv/ and web/node_modules/ were correctly skipped as gitignored.

normalization_notes.observation: osv-scanner normalises the PyPI version 5.1 to 5.1.0
normalization_notes.detail: backend/requirements.txt pins `pyyaml==5.1`, but osv-scanner reports package.version as '5.1.0'. Any ARVE fingerprint built from (package, version) will therefore key on 5.1.0, not the 5.1 written in the lockfile. This is not a bug in either tool, but it must be handled deliberately: a naive diff of ARVE output against the raw lockfile text will not match, and a fingerprint that later switches between the two forms would resolve-and-reopen every PyYAML finding.
All six npm packages report the exact version string from package-lock.json.
